column5: Ngcongco (GHA VI, 1989) presents the Mfecane/Difaqane as an early 19th century revolution from the northern Nguni, caused mainly by population growth (maize adopted in the 18th century, limits to grazing and land), the Madlathule famine (dated only 'between the 1790s and 1800s', chronology uncertain), and rulers' control of production and reproduction through age regiments (Dingiswayo, Shaka); he rejects the claim that Dingiswayo copied Europeans as 'blatantly racist', and the trekboer-pressure explanation is questioned; the chapter notes the Boers 'embarked on enslavement under the device of apprenticeship'. This is the established Omer-Cooper line; whether it reports the later 'Mfecane' revision debate must be read in the next chunks. Module 7: causes stated as multi-factor and debated [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-006 chunk 2 (Ndwandwe, Mthethwa, Swazi before Shaka)
column5: Ngcongco: three big northern Nguni powers before Shaka (Ngwane-Dlamini under Sobhuza, Ndwandwe under Zwide from about 1790, Mthethwa under Dingiswayo); the age-regiment system was already general in the region and Sotho-Tswana influence (circumcision/initiation controlled by the centre) is named; Zwide drove Sobhuza north, forming the Swazi, whose age-regiments mixed Sotho clans; Dingiswayo ended circumcision seclusion, allied with Maputo (guns from Maputo, not Portuguese soldiers per Fynn), tribute from over 30 chiefdoms, killed by Zwide in 1818; Shaka then absorbed the Mthethwa into the Zulu state. Trade with Delagoa Bay (ivory) as a motive is 'still very much in debate' (Wilson, Smith). So Shaka did not invent the regiments: he used a system already in use. Module 7 (Zulu): say Shaka built on Mthethwa and Ndwandwe foundations [PROBABLE].

Shaka's innovations per Ngcongco: short stabbing spear, long shield, barefoot, regiments in barracks, celibacy until discharged, killed or fully incorporated rulers of conquered groups; he beat Zwide in 1819 and 1820; Zwide's generals Soshangane (Gaza, from near Delagoa Bay, capital Chaimaite, control of Delagoa Bay trade), Zwangendaba and Nqaba fled north; Ndebele under Mzilikazi (b. 1796; Khumalo; fled Shaka after 1822 with about 200 people; Transvaal 1824-37; Bulawayo from 1838; died 1868) built a regimental kingdom of about 20,000 soldiers with three social strata (Zansi, Enhla, Hole); sons joined fathers' regiments; Gaza used conquered Tsonga as front-line troops. Numbers are Ngcongco's/Bryant-based and the chapter flags the Fynn-derived sources. Module 7: use the Gaza/Ndebele states as Mfecane outcomes, with dates [PROBABLE].

Moshoeshoe built Lesotho from refugees at flat-topped mountain forts (Butha-Buthe, then Thaba Bosiu in 1824, about 500 ha), beat Matiwane's Ngwane in 1827, kept tribute diplomacy with neighbours and Shaka, and became 'a nation of mounted gunmen' against Griqua and Koranna raiders; he used French missionaries (1833, Morija) for defence and arms contacts and later asked Britain for annexation (1868, died 1870) to avoid the Orange Free State; Mohlomi's influence is 'possible to exaggerate'. Sebetwane's Kololo wandered after the Tlokwa attack, were beaten at Dithakong by Griqua guns in 1823, defeated the Ngwaketse (1824) and finally conquered the Lozi on the Zambezi, ruling by marriage and consultation. Module 7: Lesotho's founding shows Mfecane-era state formation by refuge and defence, not only conquest [PROBABLE].

Ngcongco's conclusion: causes were population growth and land shortage, drier climate (dendro-climatological), the Madlathule drought, and possibly the Delagoa Bay trade 'more than scholars have been willing to consider'; the impetus 'derived entirely from internal sources'; he divides the states into aggressive militarist ones (Zulu, Ndebele, Gaza, trans-Zambezi Nguni such as Zwangendaba's Jere who killed the last Mambo Chirisamhuru, crossed the Zambezi 20 November 1835, and the Maseko in Songea) and defensive ones (Lesotho, Swazi, Kololo); he says the wars reduced populations in Natal and the Orange Free State and left the region weaker for the 'second Mfecane' of Boer land seizure. The chapter does not mention the revisionist argument that the Mfecane was exaggerated or that colonial slave raiding drove it, only trade as a factor; so it presents the older Omer-Cooper thesis with a trade addition. The course should say 'the causes are debated' and not state Shaka's role as sole cause [CONTESTED].
